# Projects (section: projects)
## Job Board [Full-stack]
Two-sided job platform that matches jobs to your resume. Job seekers upload a resume, get jobs from LinkedIn, Indeed, Naukri, Glassdoor and free job APIs ranked by match %, apply to jobs posted on the site and track every application from Saved to Offer. Employers post jobs and review applicants ranked by how well their resume fits. Closed jobs are detected and removed automatically.
Stack: Java 21, Spring Boot 3.5, Spring Security, JWT, JPA, React 18, Vite, PostgreSQL, Docker, GitHub Actions
Code: https://github.com/guruprasadgp22/Job-Board
Live demo: https://job-board-6ev5.onrender.com/ (free server: the first load can take ~30 seconds)
API docs: https://job-board-6ev5.onrender.com/swagger-ui.html
Write-up: https://guruprasadgp.netlify.app/writing/job-board-matching/
Code worth reading: RelevanceScorer.java (Service logic: how each job gets its 0–100 match score) https://github.com/guruprasadgp22/Job-Board/blob/main/backend/src/main/java/com/guru/jobboard/service/RelevanceScorer.java; JwtAuthFilter.java (Security: the filter that checks the JWT on every request) https://github.com/guruprasadgp22/Job-Board/blob/main/backend/src/main/java/com/guru/jobboard/security/JwtAuthFilter.java; RelevanceAndLinkTests.java (Tests: scoring rules and closed-job detection) https://github.com/guruprasadgp22/Job-Board/blob/main/backend/src/test/java/com/guru/jobboard/RelevanceAndLinkTests.java
When: October 2026
Problem: Job hunting means checking LinkedIn, Naukri, Indeed and company pages one by one, guessing which roles actually fit, and losing track of where you applied. Job Board brings jobs into one place, scores each one against your resume, shows which required skills you have and which you're missing, and tracks every application. Employers get the other side: post a job and see applicants ranked by resume fit.
Architecture:
  - React 18 frontend (Vite · served by Spring Boot): Dashboard, ranked job search, the application board (Saved → Applied → Interviewing → Offer), profile and resume upload, and employer screens for postings and applicants. Why: Spring Boot serves the React build, so the whole app ships as one deployable unit on one URL.
  - Spring Security + JWT (BCrypt · roles): Email and password accounts with BCrypt-hashed passwords; every request carries a JWT. Job seekers and employers get separate, role-protected endpoints. Why: Stateless tokens keep each user's jobs, resume and applications private without server sessions.
  - Resume parser (PDFBox · skill catalog): Reads PDF, DOCX or pasted resumes and pulls out skills using a catalog of 165 technologies and their spellings (reactjs → React, k8s → Kubernetes). Why: Normalised skill names make matching reliable when resumes and job ads word things differently.
  - Job sync (6 sources): Pulls jobs from Remotive, RemoteOK, Arbeitnow and The Muse, plus LinkedIn, Indeed, Naukri and Glassdoor through the JSearch API and Adzuna, using your desired role and top skills as search terms. Why: Those sites forbid scraping, so jobs come from official APIs, plus a one-click bookmarklet that saves the job you're viewing.
  - Match scorer (0–100 per job): Scores each job on keyword hits and the share of its required skills found on your resume, with bonuses for preferred location and role and penalties for a seniority mismatch. Why: Showing ✓ matched and missing skills on every job explains the score instead of just ranking.
  - Cleanup (link checker): Re-checks job links and deletes a job (and its application data) when the page returns 404/410 or says the role is closed or filled. Why: Pages that block the checker (403, 429, timeouts) are retried later, never deleted, so open jobs aren't lost by mistake.
  - PostgreSQL (JPA): Stores users, jobs, employer postings, applications and preferences, and remembers removed jobs so the next sync doesn't add them back. Why: Users, jobs and applications are linked records, which a relational database models directly.
  - GitHub Actions (cron every 6 hours): Wakes the app and runs job sync for every user, then cleanup. Why: Render's free instances sleep after 15 minutes idle, so the app's own schedule can't be relied on.
  - Docker on Render (one image): Builds the frontend and backend into one image and runs it on Render, with secrets passed as environment variables. Why: One image and one service keep hosting free and simple, and no secret ever lands in the repo.
Challenges:
- Getting jobs from LinkedIn, Naukri and Indeed without scraping them: official APIs where they exist, and a bookmarklet that reads the job page you're on
- Designing a match score that's fair: keyword weight by where a skill appears, a minimum of five skills so a two-skill job can't hit 100%, and seniority penalties
- Deciding safely when a job has closed: delete on 404/410 or a "no longer accepting applications" message, but never on a blocked or slow page
- Protecting the free JSearch quota with a minimum gap between identical searches
- Keeping jobs fresh on a free host that sleeps, by waking it from a GitHub Actions cron
Status: Live on Render with code on GitHub. Seekers and employers can sign up, match, apply and track today. On the free plan, the first load after the app has slept takes 30–60 seconds.

## FlightWise AI [Full-stack]
Flight booking platform built as Spring Boot microservices. Travellers search flights in plain English or with filters, book with their seats held while they pay, and manage trips with PDF e-tickets and calendar reminders. A separate admin console manages flights, bookings, payments and users, with revenue, booking and occupancy dashboards.
Stack: Java 21, Spring Boot, Spring Cloud Gateway, Eureka, JWT, PostgreSQL, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Material UI, Docker
Code: https://github.com/guruprasadgp22/flightwise-ai
When: June 2026 – present
Problem: Booking a flight usually means filling in the same search form over and over and comparing results by hand. FlightWise AI lets travellers type what they want, like “Bangalore to Delhi tomorrow under 6000”, and get exactly that, then filter by price, departure time and airline and sort by cheapest, fastest, earliest or latest. Booking takes under a minute: saved details fill themselves in, seats are held while you pay, and every trip lives in one place with PDF e-tickets, calendar reminders and one-click cancellation. Admins get their own console to run flights, bookings, payments and users.
Architecture:
  - Customer site (React · Vite · Tailwind CSS): Home with the plain-English Ask bar and popular routes, flight search with filters and sorting, booking, My Bookings, profile, and light and dark themes. Why: Plain-English search is a rule-based parser that runs in the browser and turns a sentence into filters, so it needs no external AI service or API key.
  - Admin console (React · Material UI): Separate admin-only app: dashboard with revenue, booking and payment-status charts and flight occupancy, plus pages to manage flights, bookings, payments and users. Why: Keeping admin tools in their own app means customers never download admin code, and every admin route is still checked on the server.
  - Spring Cloud Gateway (JWT · access rules): The only entry point. It verifies every JWT, checks each route as public, logged-in or admin-only, and passes the caller's identity on to the services. Why: Security is enforced once at the edge, and internal endpoints such as seat reservation are blocked from outside entirely.
  - Eureka (service discovery): Each service registers itself, and the gateway looks up where to send traffic. Why: No hard-coded hosts or ports, so services can restart or move without config changes.
  - Auth service (accounts · roles): Registration, login, JWT and refresh tokens, profiles, and admin user management. Why: Passwords are BCrypt-hashed, and only an admin can create another admin.
  - Flight service (flights · seats): Flights, search and seat inventory. Why: Seats are reserved with one conditional SQL UPDATE, so a flight can never be oversold.
  - Booking service (bookings · holds): Creates bookings, holds seats while the traveller pays, releases them if the hold expires, and handles cancellation. Why: Each booking is checked against its owner, so users can only see or cancel their own trips.
  - Payment service (payments · refunds): Takes payments and refunds cancelled bookings. Payments are simulated in this demo. Why: The amount is always read from the booking on the server, and a booking can only be paid once.
  - Notification service (emails): Sends booking confirmation and cancellation emails. Why: Email is best-effort: if sending fails, the booking still goes through.
  - Dashboard service (admin stats): Collects the numbers behind the admin dashboard from the other services. Why: The admin console gets everything in one call instead of querying every service itself.
  - PostgreSQL (database per service): Each business service has its own database, with tables created by migrations. Why: Services stay independent: one service's schema changes can't break another.
  - Docker Compose (one command): Builds and starts every service, both front ends and the database together. Why: The whole system runs on any machine with one command.
Challenges:
- Stopping overselling: seat reservation is one conditional SQL UPDATE, so 10 parallel requests for the last 5 seats produce exactly 5 bookings
- Holding seats while the traveller pays, and releasing them automatically if the payment isn't finished in time
- Making payments tamper-proof: the amount is always taken from the booking on the server, and a booking can only be paid once
- Cancelling a paid booking refunds it and releases its seats exactly once, even if cancel is pressed twice
- Turning sentences like “Bangalore to Delhi tomorrow under 6000 for 2” into search filters with a rule-based parser that runs in the browser
- Keeping the admin console admin-only: the gateway verifies every JWT and checks the role on each route
Status: Complete and running locally with Docker Compose. One command starts every service, both front ends and the database. There's no live demo yet, so the screenshots below are from a local run; payments are simulated.

## AI Dental Condition Detection [AI / ML]
Dentes, a web app that screens panoramic dental X-rays. A YOLOv5 model marks caries, deep caries, impacted teeth and peripheral lesions with colour-coded boxes, and you get a findings summary and a report you can print or save as a PDF. Sign in with Google or email; results are deleted automatically after 24 hours.
Stack: Python, YOLOv5, PyTorch, ONNX Runtime, OpenCV, Flask, Firebase Auth, JavaScript, Docker
Code: https://github.com/guruprasadgp22/Dental-Condition-Detection-System
When: April 2026 – present
Problem: Spotting caries, deep caries, impacted teeth and peripheral lesions on a panoramic X-ray takes time and a trained eye. Dentes lets you upload an X-ray and, in about two seconds, see each finding boxed and labelled with the model's confidence, a summary with the highest-priority finding, and a printable report. It's a screening aid, not a medical diagnosis.
Architecture:
  - Web pages (Flask templates · JavaScript): Home, Scan X-ray, Conditions, Profile and a printable report. Upload by drag-and-drop, click or paste (JPG/PNG up to 10 MB) or try a sample, adjust the confidence threshold, then explore the result: show or hide each condition, toggle boxes and labels, and hover a finding to highlight it. Why: Plain pages with light and dark mode keep the home page to about 110 KB, down from more than 20 MB of GIFs.
  - Firebase Auth (Google or email): Sign in with Google or email, create an account and reset a forgotten password. Scanning and the profile page need a signed-in user. Why: Secure accounts without running an auth server, and Firestore rules let each user read and edit only their own profile.
  - Flask server (Python · gunicorn): Receives the X-ray, runs detection, saves the marked image and findings, and serves the report page. A cleanup step deletes results older than 24 hours. Why: A small Python server keeps the model, image handling and pages in one app, and old scans don't pile up.
  - YOLOv5 model (trained in PyTorch): Detects four classes on panoramic X-rays: caries, deep caries, impacted tooth and peripheral lesion. Why: A one-stage detector finds and labels every region in a single pass, fast enough for a result in about two seconds.
  - ONNX Runtime (inference): Runs the model exported from PyTorch to ONNX, picking CPU, CUDA or Apple MPS automatically. Why: Hosting needs no PyTorch, so the server uses about 250 MB of RAM and fits on a free plan.
  - OpenCV (image processing): Reads the uploaded X-ray and produces the marked image you can download. Why: Fast, well-tested image handling in Python with a headless build for servers.
  - Docker (Render-ready): A Dockerfile and a Render blueprint (render.yaml) build and run the app on any Docker host. Why: One image runs the same everywhere, and a git push can redeploy it.
Challenges:
- Exporting the YOLOv5 model to ONNX so the server runs without PyTorch in about 250 MB of RAM
- Cutting the home page from more than 20 MB of GIFs to about 110 KB
- Building an interactive viewer: colour-coded boxes, per-condition show/hide, and hover-to-highlight
- Keeping scans private: results are deleted after 24 hours, recent scans stay in the browser, and each user can only read their own profile
- Making upload easy and safe: drag-and-drop, click or paste, a built-in sample, and a 10 MB limit
Status: Working end to end locally: sign in, upload a panoramic X-ray, get marked findings in about two seconds, and print or save the report. The Docker and Render setup is ready, but there's no live demo yet. It's a screening aid, not a medical diagnosis.
